title: Cardiac AL Amyloidosis Staging (AL-ISS 2026)
stem:
A 68-year-old female with newly confirmed systemic AL amyloidosis undergoes baseline staging. Echocardiography demonstrates concentric ventricular thickening with 'apical sparing' and an abnormal global longitudinal strain (GLS) of -7%. Laboratory investigations are shown below.

According to the AL International Staging System (AL-ISS) adopted in the 2026 BSH Guideline, what is the patient's cardiac stage and projected median survival?
labData: Troponin T: 0.052 µg/L (= 52 ng/L; staging threshold 0.035 µg/L)
options: Stage II; Median survival not reached at 5 years
Stage IIIA; Median survival approximately 76 months
Stage IIIB; Median survival approximately 26 months
Stage IIIC; Median survival approximately 4 months
Stage IV; Median survival less than 1 month
rationale:
According to the 2026 BSH AL Amyloidosis Guideline (Garg et al., Table 2) and the newly adopted AL-ISS system (Khwaja et al. 2026):
• Stage IIIB is defined by NT-proBNP >8500 ng/L and Troponin T >=0.035 µg/L (median survival 26 months).
• Stage IIIC defines ultra-poor risk, requiring NT-proBNP >8500 ng/L, Troponin T >=0.035 µg/L AND abnormal global longitudinal strain (GLS) >-9% (median survival 4 months).
(The guideline table prints the troponin unit as 'ng/L'; 0.035 µg/L = 35 ng/L.)
Because this patient has NT-proBNP 9450, TnT 0.052, and GLS -7% (which is >-9%), she fulfills Stage IIIC criteria.

title: Biomarker Screening in Monoclonal Gammopathy
stem:
A 62-year-old man with known IgG lambda MGUS attends annual surveillance. He feels well with no bone pain, weight loss, or dyspnoea. His serum paraprotein is stable at 5 g/L and free light chain ratio is 0.18. Routine annual screening is performed.

Which combination of screening investigations and findings should raise immediate suspicion of presymptomatic AL amyloidosis according to the 2026 BSH Guideline?
labData: Serum Albumin: 38 g/L (down from 45 g/L 12 months ago)
options: Findings are benign MGUS; repeat in 12 months as paraprotein is stable
Concordant rise in urine PCR >50 and ACR >30 with NT-proBNP >332 ng/L indicates early renal and cardiac AL involvement; perform fat pad/bone marrow Congo red
Isolated rise in NT-proBNP indicates hypertension; refer to cardiology and continue routine haematology follow-up
Refer for immediate emergency autologous stem cell transplant
Perform renal biopsy immediately as first-line investigation before any bone marrow or fat pad testing
rationale:
The 2026 BSH Guideline (Recommendations for MGUS Monitoring, Grade 1A) states:
1. Urine PCR, ACR, and NT-proBNP should be added to standard tests for assessment as well as monitoring of MGUS.
2. Suspect kidney involvement if urine PCR >50 mg/mmol with a concordant rise in ACR >30 mg/mmol.
3. Suspect cardiac involvement if NT-proBNP >332 ng/L (in MGUS/myeloma clinics).
4. Falling albumin levels and raised ALP should prompt immediate investigation.
5. In suspected AL, abdominal fat pad aspirate or bone marrow biopsy with Congo red should be performed before invasive renal biopsy (Grade 2B).
guidelineSection: Section: When to Suspect AL Amyloidosis in MGUS / Table 1

title: Autonomic Neuropathy & Coagulopathy in Amyloidosis
stem:
A 65-year-old male presents with lightheadedness on standing, chronic nocturnal diarrhoea, and extensive spontaneous periorbital ecchymoses ('raccoon eyes'). Lying BP is 138/84 mmHg, which falls to 102/64 mmHg at 3 minutes of standing with a heart rate change from 68 to 72 bpm. Coagulation screen shows prolongation of both PT (19s) and APTT (46s) with normal fibrinogen and platelets; Factor X activity is 18%.

According to the 2026 BSH AL Amyloidosis Guideline, what is the underlying mechanism of the ecchymoses and postural hypotension?
options: Primary idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura with vasovagal syncope
Factor X deficiency due to binding by amyloid fibrils and neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from autonomic neuropathy
Scurvy with adrenal insufficiency
Warfarin toxicity with diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Severe Von Willebrand disease with sympathetic hyperreactivity
rationale:
According to the 2026 BSH Guideline on AL Amyloidosis (Garg et al.):
• Periorbital ecchymoses (purpura) and bleeding in AL amyloidosis are classic hallmark signs caused by vascular amyloid fragility and acquired Factor X deficiency (caused by rapid clearance and adsorption of circulating Factor X onto amyloid fibrils in tissues). Factor X sits in the common pathway, so its deficiency prolongs BOTH the PT and the APTT.
• Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is defined as a sustained fall in blood pressure >=20/10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing with little compensatory rise in heart rate, characteristic of autonomic amyloid infiltration.
• Both bleeding due to Factor X deficiency and postural drop >20 mmHg are explicit criteria for urgent haematology clinic referral.
guidelineSection: Section: When to Refer Urgently to a Haematology Clinic / Figure 1

title: Biss 2026: Anticoagulation-Induced Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
stem: A 28-year-old woman receiving therapeutic anticoagulation with rivaroxaban for unprovoked deep vein thrombosis develops severe heavy menstrual bleeding requiring repeated hospital attendance despite first-line measures. According to the 2026 BSH/UKHCDO Good Practice Paper on multidisciplinary haematology-gynaecology care, which anticoagulant modification is recommended to reduce HMB while maintaining therapeutic anticoagulation?
options: Switch anticoagulation to apixaban or dabigatran, which have a lower incidence of HMB
Permanently discontinue all anticoagulation without haematological review
Increase the rivaroxaban dose during menses to promote clot stabilization
Switch to low-dose unfractionated heparin without monitoring
Add high-dose aspirin alongside rivaroxaban
rationale: According to the BSH/UKHCDO 2026 Good Practice Paper (Biss et al., Section on Individuals receiving anti-coagulant therapy), oral anticoagulant agents may need to be changed in treatment-resistant HMB. Apixaban or dabigatran have a lower incidence of heavy menstrual bleeding compared to rivaroxaban (an ungraded good-practice point in the text, not a formal recommendation). Complete cessation of anticoagulation carries unacceptable risk of recurrent VTE.

title: Biss 2026: Intrauterine System Expulsion in Bleeding Disorders
stem: A 17-year-old girl with severe Type 1 von Willebrand disease is considering a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNS-IUS / Mirena) for persistent heavy menstrual bleeding. Which clinical counseling point is emphasized in the 2026 BSH/UKHCDO guideline?
options: Women with inherited bleeding disorders have higher IUS expulsion rates, and menstrual suppression can reduce this risk
LNS-IUS is strictly contraindicated in all women with inherited bleeding disorders
The device must only be inserted after full surgical hysterectomy
Coagulation factor concentrates are contraindicated during intrauterine procedures
Expulsion rates are zero in adolescent bleeding disorder populations
rationale: The BSH/UKHCDO 2026 guideline highlights that there are reports of increased intrauterine device expulsion rates in women with inherited bleeding disorders (IBDs). The role of medical menstrual suppression to decrease this expulsion risk has been described and should be discussed with the patient.
guidelineSection: Section: Individuals with inherited bleeding disorders

title: Biss 2026: PALM-COEIN Classification for Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
stem: A 22-year-old female presents to the combined clinic with menorrhagia since menarche and family history of easy bruising. According to the FIGO PALM-COEIN classification adopted by BSH/UKHCDO 2026, which category does an underlying von Willebrand disease represent?
options: Coagulopathy (Non-structural cause)
Adenomyosis (Structural cause)
Leiomyoma (Structural cause)
Endometrial (Structural cause)
Iatrogenic (Structural cause)
rationale: In the FIGO PALM-COEIN system adopted in the BSH/UKHCDO guideline, PALM represents structural etiologies (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy), whereas COEIN represents non-structural etiologies (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). Inherited bleeding disorders fall under Coagulopathy.

title: Tam 2026: Point-of-Care D-Dimer for VTE Exclusion
stem: An ambulatory care unit is evaluating a bedside point-of-care test for D-dimer to aid in the exclusion of deep vein thrombosis. According to the 2026 BSH Point-of-Care Testing guideline (Tam et al.), what is the specific recommendation regarding POCT D-dimer assays?
options: Only high-sensitivity D-dimer tests with performance matching STA or ELISA laboratory assays should be used (Grade 1B)
Qualitative POCT D-dimer dipstick assays are sufficient to exclude PE in high-risk patients
Any POCT D-dimer device may be used without comparison to laboratory reference methods
D-dimer testing should be replaced entirely by bedside ultrasound without clinical pre-test probability scoring
POCT D-dimer has higher sensitivity than automated central laboratory latex immunoassays
rationale: According to the 2026 BSH POCT guideline recommendation (Grade 1B), only high-sensitivity D-dimer tests with performance matching STA or ELISA laboratory assays should be used. Meta-analyses have shown that qualitative POCT D-dimer assays have limited utility due to low sensitivity and must not be used to rule out VTE.

title: Tam 2026: Blood Gas Analysers vs Central Laboratory Haemoglobin
stem: In an emergency department, a patient with upper GI bleeding has a blood gas analyser (BGA) haemoglobin of 72 g/L. The central laboratory full blood count returns a haemoglobin of 84 g/L. According to the 2026 BSH Point-of-Care Testing guideline, what is the key clinical guidance regarding BGAs?
options: Blood gas analysers should not substitute laboratory-based testing of Hb/Hct but may aid in monitoring trends (Grade 1C)
BGAs are fully interchangeable with central laboratory analysers under CLIA criteria
BGA haemoglobin measurements are unaffected by haemolysis or lipaemia
Blood transfusion should always be triggered solely by BGA without laboratory verification
Centrifugal BGA methods consistently overestimate haemoglobin compared to central laboratories
rationale: The BSH 2026 guideline explicitly recommends that blood gas analysers should not substitute laboratory-based testing of Hb/Hct (Grade 1C). Studies disagree in both directions: BGA underestimation can trigger unnecessary transfusion, while one study found 21% of patients who would be transfused on the lab Hct would not be on the BGA Hct, and another found systematic BGA overestimation (mean 8 g/L). BGAs are therefore not interchangeable with lab analysers.

title: Tam 2026: POCT PT/INR Limitations in Antiphospholipid Syndrome
stem: A 42-year-old woman with triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome on warfarin attends a clinic where an electromechanical POCT PT/INR meter (CoaguChek) reports an INR of 2.4. Which limitation of POCT PT/INR devices is highlighted in the 2026 BSH guideline?
options: Clinically significant discrepancies occur in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome receiving warfarin, requiring central laboratory monitoring
POCT PT/INR devices are completely immune to lupus anticoagulant interference
POCT meters are accurate up to INR 12.0 without lot-to-lot bias
POCT PT/INR is licensed for direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) therapeutic drug monitoring
Capillary INR is identical to venous laboratory INR in all thrombophilia conditions
rationale: The 2026 BSH guideline notes that despite widespread use, portable PT/INR devices have notable limitations: clinically significant discrepancies have been observed in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome receiving warfarin. In addition, at INRs >=4, analytical bias exists between test strip lots.
guidelineSection: Section: Point-of-care PT/INR testing for anticoagulation management

title: MacDonald 2026: Emergency Suspicion & Sample Requirements for TTP
stem: A 34-year-old previously well woman presents to the acute medical unit with confusion, petechiae, a platelet count of 18 x 10^9/L, and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with abundant schistocytes. Which statement accurately reflects the 2026 BSH laboratory guideline (MacDonald et al.)?
options: Suspected TTP is a medical emergency: ADAMTS13 activity availability is not a prerequisite for initiating treatment, and pre-treatment blood must be collected in 0.109 M sodium citrate
Plasma exchange must be withheld until quantitative ADAMTS13 activity confirmation is received
Blood samples for ADAMTS13 activity should be collected into EDTA tubes to stabilize metalloproteinase cleavage
Blood film review for thrombocytopenia with haemolysis should be deferred until the next routine laboratory shift
An ADAMTS13 activity of 25 IU/dL confirms acute immune-mediated TTP
rationale: The BSH 2026 guideline emphasizes that suspected TTP is a medical emergency where availability of ADAMTS13 activity is NOT a prerequisite for immediate treatment (stated as context, ungraded). Samples should be collected into 0.109 M (3.2%) sodium citrate BEFORE treatment (Grade 1B). EDTA cannot be used because it chelates divalent cations (zinc and calcium), causing falsely low ADAMTS13 activity.
guidelineSection: Section: Laboratory Investigation for TTP & Pre-analytical considerations

title: MacDonald 2026: ADAMTS13 Activity Cutoff & Turnaround Standards
stem: According to the 2026 BSH laboratory guideline for TTP, which ADAMTS13 activity threshold confirms the diagnosis of TTP, and what is the recommended turnaround time for rapid automated assays in suspected cases?
options: ADAMTS13 activity <10 IU/dL confirms TTP; preliminary results should be available ideally within 1 hour of sample receipt (Grade 1C)
ADAMTS13 activity <50 IU/dL confirms TTP; preliminary results within 24 hours
ADAMTS13 activity <30 IU/dL confirms TTP; preliminary results within 12 hours
ADAMTS13 activity <5 IU/dL confirms TTP; results are only valid if tested by manual full-length VWF multimer assay
ADAMTS13 activity <20 IU/dL confirms TTP; turnaround times of up to 48 hours are acceptable
rationale: The 2026 BSH guideline states that ADAMTS13 activity <10 IU/dL is the diagnostic cut-off for TTP (10–20 IU/dL is an equivocal grey zone for manual FRET/ELISA assays; not established for automated platforms). In suspected TTP, preliminary results should be available as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of sample receipt for rapid automated assays, or 6 hours for ELISA (Grade 1C).
guidelineSection: Section: Turnaround Times & Testing for ADAMTS13 Activity

title: MacDonald 2026: Anti-ADAMTS13 Antibody Timing and Methodology
stem: In a patient with confirmed severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (<10 IU/dL), what does the 2026 BSH guideline mandate regarding anti-ADAMTS13 antibody testing?
options: Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody assays must be performed within 72 hours of presentation, and an ELISA is recommended over Bethesda-style inhibitor assays (Grade 1B/2D)
Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody testing is unnecessary in acute TTP
Bethesda-style inhibitor assays are superior to ELISA for detecting non-neutralising antibodies
Antibody testing should only be performed after 6 months of clinical remission
Presence of anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies confirms congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome)
rationale: The 2026 BSH guideline recommends that anti-ADAMTS13 antibody assays must be performed within 72h of presentation when ADAMTS13 activity is <10 IU/dL (Grade 1B). An ELISA is recommended over non-standardised Bethesda-style inhibitor assays or mixing studies because ELISA detects both neutralising and non-neutralising IgG antibodies (Grade 2D).
guidelineSection: Recommendations: Testing for antibodies against ADAMTS13

title: Osborne 2026: Omission of Radiotherapy in Complete Metabolic Response
stem: A 26-year-old woman with newly diagnosed bulky Primary Mediastinal B-cell Lymphoma (PMBCL) completes 6 cycles of DA-R-EPOCH. An end-of-treatment PET-CT scan performed at 6 weeks demonstrates Deauville Score 2 (Complete Metabolic Response). According to the 2026 BSH guideline (Osborne et al.) and the IELSG37 prospective trial, what is the recommended management?
options: Do not offer consolidative radiotherapy; observation only is recommended (Grade 1A)
Mandatory consolidative involved-site radiotherapy to 36 Gy regardless of PET response
Immediate autologous stem cell transplantation as consolidation
Maintenance rituximab for 2 years
High-dose salvage chemotherapy with R-ICE
rationale: The 2026 BSH PMBCL guideline states: 'Do not offer radiotherapy for patients with DS 1–3 following chemoimmunotherapy (Grade 1A)'. This is supported by the landmark IELSG37 trial, which randomised patients in complete metabolic response (DS 1–3) to observation vs radiotherapy and showed no survival detriment with observation (5-year OS 99% in both arms).
guidelineSection: Recommendations: Radiotherapy consolidation after first-line chemoimmunotherapy

title: Osborne 2026: First-Line Chemoimmunotherapy Regimens
stem: A 32-year-old man is diagnosed with anterior mediastinal PMBCL with superior vena cava compression. Which first-line chemotherapy approach is recommended by the 2026 BSH guideline?
options: Offer dose-intensive R-CHOP-14 x6 or DA-R-EPOCH x6; R-CHOP-21 is not recommended (Grade 1B)
R-CHOP-21 for 6 cycles is the preferred national standard of care
Single-agent rituximab with involved-field radiation therapy
CHOP-21 chemotherapy without anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody
Immediate upfront CAR T-cell therapy without prior chemoimmunotherapy
rationale: The 2026 BSH guideline recommends dose-intensive chemoimmunotherapy: offer R-CHOP-14 x6 or DA-R-EPOCH x6 (Grade 1B). In the IELSG37 trial (not powered to compare induction regimens), patients given R-CHOP-21 had a significantly higher rate of Deauville 5 response (23.8% vs 8.2%) and inferior EFS compared with dose-intensive regimens; R-CHOP-21 is therefore not recommended (Grade 1B). A LYSA study found no efficacy difference between R-CHOP-14 and DA-R-EPOCH but more toxicity with DA-R-EPOCH.

title: Osborne 2026: Thromboprophylaxis & Second-Line CAR T-Cell Therapy
stem: Which pair of recommendations is explicitly supported in the 2026 BSH PMBCL guideline?
options: Thromboprophylaxis is recommended at presentation in patients with platelets >50 x 10^9/L (Grade 1C), and CD19 CAR T-cell therapy (liso-cel) is recommended for relapse within 12 months (Grade 1C)
Anticoagulation is strictly contraindicated in PMBCL due to pericardial effusion risk, and autologous transplant is superior to CAR-T in primary refractory disease
Surveillance PET-CT imaging should be performed every 3 months for 5 years in asymptomatic patients
Central nervous system prophylaxis is mandatory in all PMBCL patients
R-CHOP-21 is superior to DA-R-EPOCH in women under 40
rationale: The 2026 BSH PMBCL guideline emphasizes two crucial points: (1) Thrombotic complications occur in 28% of patients (most often around presentation); thromboprophylaxis is recommended if platelets >50 x 10^9/L (Grade 1C). (2) In patients with relapsed or refractory disease within 12 months, second-line high-dose chemotherapy has very poor outcomes; CD19 CAR T-cell therapy (liso-cel, TRANSFORM trial) is licensed and recommended second-line (Grade 1C). Routine surveillance imaging in asymptomatic patients in remission is not recommended (Grade 1B).

title: AML presenting in the late second trimester
stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation is diagnosed with AML (normal karyotype, NPM1-mutated). She is clinically well. She asks whether she should be delivered before starting treatment.

According to the BCSH guideline on AML in pregnancy, what is the most appropriate approach?
options: Deliver by caesarean section now, then start induction chemotherapy
Delay chemotherapy until 32 weeks, then deliver and treat
Recommend termination of pregnancy before chemotherapy
Start induction chemotherapy without delay and continue the pregnancy, with any change in delivery timing decided by the MDT
Give hydroxycarbamide until 36 weeks, then deliver and give definitive treatment
rationale: Between 24 and 28 weeks the fetal risks of prematurity are high, and chemotherapy appears to carry a low fetal risk. Delivery is therefore not usually advised and treatment should not be delayed (treat without delay, 1B). Between 24 and 32 weeks, the risks of chemotherapy exposure must be balanced against prematurity (1C), and decisions to delay delivery to a critical gestation (e.g. 26 weeks) should be taken by the MDT. Termination is discussed for first-trimester diagnoses. Delivery before chemotherapy is considered beyond 32 weeks. Hydroxycarbamide is avoided except with WBC >100 × 10⁹/l.
guidelineSection: Issues of management in the second and third trimesters
yearPaper: BCSH 2015 AML in pregnancy (Ali et al.)

title: Choice of induction regimen in pregnancy
stem:
A woman at 20 weeks gestation is starting induction for newly diagnosed AML. She has gained 6 kg since booking.

Which induction plan is recommended?
options: Daunorubicin 60 mg/m² d1,3,5 with cytarabine 100 mg/m² 12-hourly d1–10, dosed on current actual body weight
Idarubicin 12 mg/m² d1–3 with cytarabine 100 mg/m² CI d1–7, dosed on ideal body weight
Daunorubicin 90 mg/m² d1,3,5 with cytarabine, dosed on booking weight
Azacitidine plus venetoclax to avoid anthracycline exposure
Single-agent cytarabine until delivery
rationale: The BCSH guideline recommends standard daunorubicin and cytarabine '3 + 10' (daunorubicin 60 mg/m² d1,3,5; cytarabine 100 mg/m² 12-hourly d1–10) (1B), dosed on actual body weight with adjustments for weight change (1C). There are no data supporting daunorubicin 90 mg/m² in pregnancy. Idarubicin is more lipophilic, crosses the placenta more readily, and has been associated with transient neonatal cardiomyopathy.
yearPaper: BCSH 2015 AML in pregnancy (Ali et al.)

title: Neutropenic fever in pregnancy
stem: A woman at 23 weeks gestation develops neutropenic fever after induction for AML. She is haemodynamically stable. The ward pharmacist asks which empirical antibiotic plan avoids drugs the BCSH guideline advises against in pregnancy.
options: Co-amoxiclav plus gentamicin
Ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole
Levofloxacin monotherapy
Doxycycline plus co-trimoxazole
Piperacillin–tazobactam (with gentamicin if needed)
rationale: Penicillins, erythromycin, metronidazole and cephalosporins are safe. If sepsis is suspected, clindamycin, piperacillin–tazobactam, carbapenems and gentamicin can all be used (relatively limited data for aminoglycosides). Quinolones, Augmentin (co-amoxiclav, because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis), tetracyclines and sulphonamides should be avoided (1B).
yearPaper: BCSH 2015 AML in pregnancy (Ali et al.)

title: Analgesia for labour in AML
stem:
A woman with AML in remission after two cycles of chemotherapy is being induced at 37 weeks. Her counts are shown below.

Which statement about her intrapartum care is correct?
options: Epidural analgesia is appropriate because her neutrophils are recovering
Caesarean section is indicated because of the leukaemia
Epidural analgesia should be avoided; pethidine or diamorphine can be used
Fetal scalp electrodes and forceps are contraindicated
Intramuscular injections are safe at this platelet count
rationale: Epidural analgesia should be avoided if platelets are <80 × 10⁹/l and/or WBC <1 × 10⁹/l (1C). Here the platelets are 45 × 10⁹/l, so use alternatives such as pethidine or diamorphine. IM injections should be avoided if platelets are <50 × 10⁹/l. Elective caesarean section is only for obstetric indications (2C). Because neonatal myelosuppression risk is low, fetal scalp sampling and electrodes, ventouse and forceps are not contraindicated.
guidelineSection: Preparation for and management of delivery
yearPaper: BCSH 2015 AML in pregnancy (Ali et al.)

title: Turnaround standard for suspected APL
stem:
A 41-year-old man presents with pancytopenia, a coagulopathy, and abundant hypergranular promyelocytes with multiple Auer rods on the film.

According to the BSH good practice paper on AML laboratory testing, what is the turnaround standard for PML::RARA testing?
options: Within 24 hours of sample receipt
Within 72 hours of sample receipt
Within 3 working days with the NGS panel
Within 7 days with the full karyotype
Within 14 days with the AML NGS panel
rationale: Where indicated, PML::RARA testing must be completed within 24 hours of sample receipt (FISH turnaround 1 day; RT-PCR 3 days). Rearrangements cryptic to both karyotype and FISH need molecular characterisation within 72 h if suspicion persists. CBF lesions are 72 h, FLT3 and NPM1 3 days, karyotype 7 days, and NGS 14 days.
yearPaper: BSH 2023 AML laboratory testing (Mehta et al.)

title: Interpreting a diagnostic AML flow report
stem:
A new AML diagnosis has favourable-risk cytogenetics. The team are considering 7 + 3 with gemtuzumab ozogamicin. The flow report gives the blast percentage and lineage but no comment on CD33.

What does the BSH guidance say?
options: CD33 status is only needed at relapse
Diagnostic reports should record whether AML cells are CD33 positive; GO can work even with weak or partial CD33
GO is contraindicated unless >90% of blasts are strongly CD33 positive
CD33 should be inferred from the karyotype
CD123 rather than CD33 determines GO eligibility
rationale: Treatment authorisation for GO requires CD33 positivity, so all diagnostic and relapse reports should state clearly whether blasts are CD33 positive (flow recommendation 2). GO can be effective with partial or weak CD33 positivity, as seen in CBF AML. Laboratories need validated thresholds and should take part in EQA (UK NEQAS Leukaemia Immunophenotyping Part 1). CD123 is relevant for tagraxofusp in BPDCN.
yearPaper: BSH 2023 AML laboratory testing (Mehta et al.)

title: Blast thresholds under different classifications
stem:
A marrow shows 14% myeloblasts with an NPM1 mutation and no other abnormality.

Which statement is correct?
options: This is MDS under both WHO 2022 and ICC 2022
MDS/AML under ICC because blasts are 10–19%
AML under WHO only if blasts reach 20%
AML under WHO 2022 (no blast cut-off for AML with defining genetic abnormalities) and AML under ICC 2022 (≥10% blasts)
AML only if CD34 is positive
rationale: In WHO 2022, a ≥20% blast count is required only for AML without defining genetic abnormalities (DGA). AML with DGA (e.g. NPM1) has no specific cut-off, except BCR::ABL1 and CEBPA. The ICC uses ≥10% for AML with DGA and reserves MDS/AML (10–19%) for cases without DGA.
yearPaper: BSH 2023 AML laboratory testing (Mehta et al.)

title: Suspected germline variant on a somatic panel
stem:
A 38-year-old woman with AML has a RUNX1 variant at 48% VAF on the diagnostic NGS panel. Her mother had "low platelets" and her uncle died of MDS. Her sibling is being HLA-typed as a potential donor.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Report the variant as somatic and proceed with the sibling donor
Repeat NGS on peripheral blood in remission and proceed if the variant persists
Test the sibling's marrow for AML
Ignore it: RUNX1 is not a germline predisposition gene
Highlight a suspected germline finding in the report and confirm on cultured skin fibroblasts, with Clinical Genetics input, before using a related donor
rationale: Driver variants found by somatic-only testing may be germline. RUNX1 is one of the high-actionability genes (with CEBPA, DDX41, ANKRD26, ETV6 and GATA2). A suspected germline finding must be clearly highlighted in the report (gen-6). Confirmation needs cultured skin fibroblasts from a skin biopsy, with a detailed family history and Clinical Genetics referral. Familial predisposition matters especially when choosing a related donor. A remission blood sample cannot prove germline status.
yearPaper: BSH 2023 AML laboratory testing (Mehta et al.)

title: KMT2A testing strategy
stem:
A diagnostic AML sample has a normal-looking karyotype, and FLT3, NPM1 and CBF tests are negative.

Which approach to KMT2A testing does the BSH recommend?
options: KMT2A testing is unnecessary if the karyotype is normal
Partner-agnostic break-apart FISH, optionally with an RNA NGS fusion panel, then identification of the partner if positive
RT-PCR for MLLT3::KMT2A only
NGS DNA panel for KMT2A point mutations
Wait for whole genome sequencing at 42 days
rationale: KMT2A rearrangements may be cryptic and are disease-defining, so testing is mandatory when no other defining genetic abnormality is found. Given the many fusion partners, a partner-agnostic approach (break-apart FISH) is essential, and an RNA NGS fusion panel may help. If a rearrangement is found, further testing should identify the partner for risk assignment (e.g. t(9;11) is intermediate, other KMT2A rearrangements adverse).
yearPaper: BSH 2023 AML laboratory testing (Mehta et al.)

title: 2022 ELN risk: NPM1 and FLT3-ITD
stem:
A 52-year-old man has AML with a normal karyotype, an NPM1 mutation and a FLT3-ITD with an allelic ratio of 0.3.

What is his 2022 ELN genetic risk group?
options: Favourable, because the FLT3-ITD allelic ratio is low
Adverse
Intermediate
Favourable if he receives midostaurin
Cannot be assigned without IDH1/2 status
rationale: In ELN 2022 the FLT3-ITD allelic ratio is no longer considered. Mutated NPM1 with FLT3-ITD is intermediate risk, whatever the ratio. The reasons are difficulty standardising the assay, the effect of midostaurin, and the growing role of MRD. (NPM1 without FLT3-ITD is favourable; NPM1 with adverse cytogenetics is adverse.) IDH1/IDH2 are not assigned a risk group.

title: ICC hierarchy
stem:
A 67-year-old with no prior haematological history has 32% blasts, a complex karyotype, a TP53 mutation (VAF 41%) and an SRSF2 mutation.

What is the ICC 2022 diagnosis?
options: AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations
AML with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities
MDS/AML with mutated TP53
AML, not otherwise specified
AML with mutated TP53
rationale: The ICC is hierarchical. With no AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality, AML with mutated TP53 (pathogenic TP53 at VAF ≥10%) outranks AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations (e.g. SRSF2), which outranks MR cytogenetics. With ≥20% blasts this is AML, not MDS/AML (10–19%).

title: Response category after induction
stem:
A patient with AML has a marrow on day 35 after 7 + 3 showing 2% blasts with no circulating blasts. No G-CSF or transfusions have been given in the past 10 days.

What is the ELN 2022 response category?
options: CR
CRh
CRi
MLFS
PR
rationale: All of CR, CRh and CRi need marrow blasts <5%, no circulating blasts and no extramedullary disease. CR needs ANC ≥1.0 and platelets ≥100 × 10⁹/L. CRh needs partial recovery: ANC ≥0.5 and platelets ≥50. With ANC 0.7 and platelets 62, this meets CRh. If CRh is used, CRi is reserved for patients who do not meet CRh. Counts must be assessed without G-CSF or platelet transfusion in the preceding 7 days.

title: NPM1 MRD after induction
stem:
A 45-year-old with NPM1-mutated AML (no FLT3-ITD, normal karyotype) is in CR after 2 cycles of intensive chemotherapy.

According to ELN, which MRD finding would most support treatment modification such as allo-HCT?
options: NPM1 transcripts detectable at <2% at the end of consolidation, stable on repeat
Persistent DNMT3A mutation at 8% VAF on NGS
MFC-MRD 0.05% after cycle 2
NPM1 MRD ≥2%, or failure to achieve a 3–4 log reduction after consolidation
A qPCR Ct of 41 in all 3 replicates
rationale: Per ELN (Figure 2), molecular MRD ≥2% or failure to reduce mutant transcripts by 3–4 log after consolidation may prompt treatment changes such as allo-HCT. CR with MRD at low level (<2%) in NPM1 and CBF AML is treated as MRD negative. DNMT3A persistence reflects clonal haematopoiesis and is not MRD. MFC positivity is ≥0.1%. qPCR is negative if Ct ≥40 in ≥2 of 3 replicates.

title: Choosing an intensive regimen by genotype
stem:
A 66-year-old fit man has AML 4 years after chemoradiotherapy for a head and neck cancer. Cytogenetics show −7 and del(5q). FLT3 and NPM1 are wild type.

Which induction is best supported by ELN 2022?
options: 7 + 3 with midostaurin
7 + 3 with gemtuzumab ozogamicin
CPX-351
Single-agent oral azacitidine
High-dose cytarabine 3 g/m² monotherapy
rationale: CPX-351 (liposomal daunorubicin and cytarabine) improved response and OS (5-year 18% vs 10%) over 7 + 3 in patients aged 60–75 with therapy-related AML, AML after MDS or CMML, or de novo AML with MR cytogenetics. Midostaurin is for FLT3-mutated AML. GO benefit is limited to favourable or intermediate cytogenetics. Oral azacitidine is maintenance, not induction.
guidelineSection: Therapy: patients fit for intensive therapy

title: Venetoclax with azole prophylaxis
stem:
A 78-year-old is starting azacitidine plus venetoclax and will take posaconazole prophylaxis. Her WBC is 38 × 10⁹/L.

Which is correct?
options: Start venetoclax 400 mg daily immediately; posaconazole has no interaction
Avoid antifungal prophylaxis altogether
Halve the azacitidine dose instead of adjusting venetoclax
Use venetoclax 600 mg because azacitidine induces CYP3A
Cytoreduce to WBC <25 × 10⁹/L, give TLS prophylaxis, and ramp venetoclax 10 → 20 → 50 → ≤100 mg because posaconazole is a strong CYP3A inhibitor
rationale: Before venetoclax-based therapy, reduce the WBC to <25 × 10⁹/L (e.g. hydroxyurea) with hydration, urate-lowering drugs and electrolyte monitoring, because of tumour lysis risk. Posaconazole is a strong CYP3A inhibitor: ramp venetoclax 10 mg d1, 20 mg d2, 50 mg d3, then 100 mg or less (VIALE used 50 mg). Moderate inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin need at least a 50% reduction. ELN also recommends posaconazole prophylaxis during induction.

title: Transplant in first remission
stem:
A 40-year-old with AML with inv(16) CBFB::MYH11 and a KIT mutation is in CR after induction. Serial qPCR shows a good molecular response, with MRD-negative status at end of consolidation.

What is the ELN recommendation on allo-HCT in CR1?
options: Allo-HCT in CR1, because the KIT mutation makes this adverse risk
Allo-HCT generally not recommended in CR1, because this is favourable risk with adequate MRD clearance
Allo-HCT in CR1 for all CBF AML
Autologous HCT is mandatory
Allo-HCT after 2 more cycles of HiDAC to deepen MRD
rationale: Concurrent KIT and/or FLT3 mutations do not alter the favourable risk of CBF AML. For favourable-risk disease, allogeneic HCT in CR1 is generally not recommended except with inadequate MRD clearance. Allo-HCT is considered when predicted relapse risk exceeds 35–40% (adverse risk, or non-adverse with MRD persistence).

title: Hyperleukocytosis
stem:
A 70-year-old with newly diagnosed monocytic AML has a WBC of 162 × 10⁹/L. He is alert, with normal oxygen saturations and no visual or neurological symptoms. Venetoclax-based therapy is planned.

What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Hydroxyurea (up to 50–60 mg/kg/day) to bring the WBC below 25 × 10⁹/L, with TLS prophylaxis and a restrictive red cell transfusion policy
Urgent leukapheresis
Transfuse 2 units of red cells to correct Hb 78 g/L before cytoreduction
Start venetoclax 400 mg immediately
No action until symptoms of leukostasis appear
rationale: Hyperleukocytosis (WBC >100 × 10⁹/L) raises induction mortality through haemorrhage, TLS and leukostasis. Hydroxyurea up to 50–60 mg/kg/day is most commonly used to lower the WBC below 25 × 10⁹/L, particularly before HMA or venetoclax. Current evidence does not support leukapheresis in asymptomatic hyperleukocytosis. A restrictive red cell transfusion policy is advised.
